opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is: a lot more than people expect, but not all the way on its own.

If you look at what's happened with large language models in medicine over the last few years, the core recipe of large-scale pretraining on broad data followed by post-training with things like reinforcement learning has gotten us surprisingly far. These models went from barely passing medical licensing-style questions to performing at or above expert level on many benchmarks, and in some studies they hold their own on real diagnostic reasoning and conversations. That's a big deal, and it tells you that a lot of medical knowledge, and even some clinical reasoning, is learnable from text.

But a world model that actually predicts a specific person's health trajectory is a different kind of problem. Knowing medicine in general isn't the same as modeling *you*: your genetics, labs over time, sleep, activity, medications, environment, and how all of those interact. A few things are missing from current paradigms.

The first is data. The most predictive health data is longitudinal, multimodal, and fragmented across health systems, devices, and labs. Much of it is noisy, irregularly sampled, and locked up for good privacy reasons. Text-scale pretraining doesn't hand you that.

The second is grounding in outcomes. Today's models are mostly trained to produce responses that look good to a human rater, or that match a known answer. Health prediction needs to be anchored in what actually happened to people over months and years. That feedback loop is slow and expensive, and it makes RL-style training much harder.

The third is causality. If a world model is going to be useful, it has to answer counterfactuals: what happens if this person starts this drug, or changes their sleep? Correlational pretraining gets you part of the way, but you really need interventional data and careful evaluation to trust those answers.

So my view is that current paradigms give us an incredibly strong foundation: general reasoning, medical knowledge, and the ability to ingest and interpret messy data like notes, wearables, and imaging. On top of that you'll need new data partnerships, longitudinal and multimodal training objectives, and much more rigorous real-world evaluation, ideally prospective, before anyone should trust predictions about an individual.

The exciting part is that the pieces are starting to come together. The models are good enough that they can be the interface and the reasoning layer, and the bottleneck is increasingly the data and evaluation infrastructure rather than the model architecture. That's a very solvable kind of bottleneck, though it takes a lot of careful, unglamorous work to solve it safely.

r001.rationale: It says individual health prediction needs new longitudinal, multimodal training objectives and outcome-based feedback beyond current approaches.

r002.rationale: It frames predicting a specific person’s trajectory and intervention counterfactuals as areas where current models could progress, given richer individual data and evaluation.

r003.rationale: It describes a common core recipe of broad, large-scale pretraining followed by post-training, including reinforcement learning.

r004.rationale: It credits that recipe with past progress, but does not argue that extending pretraining and scaling reasoning-style training will continue to deliver substantial progress.

r005.rationale: It calls for new longitudinal and multimodal training objectives, so it does not convey that integrating modalities can happen without major paradigm changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that current paradigms get us a surprisingly long way, but they hit a wall that's less about model capacity and more about the data and the structure of the problem.

If you look at what we've done so far at Google with things like Med-PaLM and the work since then, the striking thing is how much medical knowledge falls out of pretraining on text. The model learns what hypertension is, how it interacts with kidney disease, what the typical trajectory looks like. That's real, and it's useful. It gives you a kind of population-level prior about health.

But a world model that predicts a specific person's health is a different object. It needs to take in longitudinal signals, things like wearables data, lab values over time, genomics, what someone's life actually looks like day to day, and reason about how those interact for that individual. And the training data for that mostly doesn't exist in the form we'd need. Health records are fragmented, they're biased toward the moments when someone was sick enough to show up, and the outcomes you care about play out over years or decades. You can't just scrape the internet for that.

So my view is that scaling the current recipe keeps improving the prior, the general medical reasoning. Where I'm less sure is whether it gets you the personalized dynamics without a shift in how we collect and structure data, and probably a shift toward models that can actively ask the right questions, run small experiments with a person, and update. That starts to look more like an agent that's learning about you over time than a static model that's been trained once.

The other piece I'd flag is that prediction alone isn't the goal. If I tell you there's a thirty percent chance of some outcome, the question is what you do about it. So the paradigm has to produce models that are calibrated, that know what they don't know, and that can communicate uncertainty to a clinician or a patient in a way that actually changes decisions. I think we're earlier on that than people assume, and it's where a lot of the interesting work is.

r001.rationale: The response says personalized health dynamics likely require changes to data collection and structure, plus models that learn about a person over time.

r002.rationale: It discusses predicting an individual’s health from extensive context, but does not identify predicting intervention outcomes as a task current models could substantially improve at.

r003.rationale: It refers to “current paradigms” and a “current recipe,” but does not suggest that training developments to date belong to one single paradigm.

r004.rationale: It says scaling the current recipe will keep improving general medical reasoning and describes current paradigms as already delivering substantial progress.

r005.rationale: It lists additional data modalities but does not say they can be integrated without major changes to current training paradigms; it instead anticipates a shift for personalized dynamics.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of room for progress with the paradigms we already have. But I’d separate two things: learning to reason about medicine from text, and learning to predict what actually happens to a person over time. Those are related, but they’re not the same task.

A model can give a very good explanation of a disease without being able to tell you, for this particular patient, what’s going to happen in six months. For that, you need longitudinal data—observations of people’s health, the treatments they receive, and their outcomes. And a lot of the relevant information isn’t captured, or it’s scattered across different systems.

There’s also a distinction between prediction and intervention. Predicting that someone is likely to get worse is useful. Knowing which action would prevent that is a harder problem, because the treatment decisions in your training data weren’t random. You can’t automatically interpret those correlations as causal effects.

So I’m optimistic that current approaches can take us substantially further, especially as we train on richer data and evaluate against real outcomes. I’m less confident that simply scaling up training on medical text gets us all the way to a reliable model of an individual’s health. That’s something we have to demonstrate empirically.

r001.rationale: The response doubts that scaling medical-text training alone will suffice, but does not say full health simulations probably require different training approaches.

r002.rationale: It describes intervention effects as harder to predict because of causal confounding, but does not clearly claim current models could substantially improve at predicting them from extensive individual context.

r003.rationale: It refers to current paradigms and approaches, but does not characterize developments to date as one single paradigm.

r004.rationale: It expects substantial progress from current approaches and richer data, but does not specifically endorse extending pre-training and scaling reasoning-style training.

r005.rationale: It mentions richer and scattered health data, but says nothing about integrating additional modalities or whether that requires major paradigm changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of progress to be made with the current paradigms. But I’d separate predicting what happens next in a medical record from predicting what will happen to a person’s health. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. A medical record reflects both the patient’s biology and the decisions people made about what to measure and how to treat them.

You can imagine training on much richer longitudinal data—what’s happened to someone over time, their labs, imaging, treatments—and getting increasingly useful predictions. The harder question is, “What would happen if we intervened differently?” That’s what you really want to know when you’re making a medical decision, and observational data doesn’t always let you answer it reliably.

So I’m optimistic that scaling the current approaches can take us substantially further. I’m less confident that a better training objective alone gets us all the way there. We’ll need better data and prospective evaluations that establish whether these predictions actually help us improve someone’s health.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current approaches may not get all the way there, but does not say full health simulations would probably require different training approaches.

r002.rationale: It describes intervention outcomes as difficult to predict reliably from observational data and does not say current models could improve substantially at that task.

r003.rationale: The candidate refers to “current paradigms” but does not characterize AI training developments to date as one single paradigm.

r004.rationale: It says scaling current approaches can make substantial progress, but does not identify extending pre-training and scaling reasoning-style training as the means.

r005.rationale: The candidate does not discuss integrating additional modalities or whether that would require changes to training paradigms.
